description:
Audit Bluetooth Classic and BLE devices: RFCOMM, GATT and advertisements

DissPair is an open-source Bluetooth security toolkit for auditing Bluetooth Classic (RFCOMM) and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) devices you own or are authorized to test. Instead of trusting what a device advertises, it actively probes how the device really behaves. Two CVEs have been found with it (CVE-2026-31280, CVE-2025-67133).

Discovery

  • Scan Classic (BR/EDR) and BLE devices, plus already-paired devices
  • Device class tags, RSSI and filters for unnamed and paired devices

Bluetooth Classic (RFCOMM)

  • Sweep RFCOMM channels 1-30 and see which accept unpaired (insecure) or paired connections
  • Send AT commands and OBEX payloads, with automatic HFP handshake handling
  • Flood test to stress a channel's buffer handling

BLE advertisement inspector (GAP)

  • Decodes every advertising field: flags, service UUIDs, names, TX power, appearance, service and manufacturer data
  • Vendor formats: Apple Continuity (iBeacon, AirDrop, Handoff, Nearby Info, Find My), Eddystone, Google Fast Pair
  • Privacy checks: public vs rotating addresses, identifiers in device names, tracker beacons (Find My, SmartTag, Tile)
  • Advertising interval estimate, RSSI graph, legacy/extended PDU, PHY and connectable flags

BLE GATT analysis

  • Full service and characteristic map with standard and vendor names
  • Read and write (with or without response), hex or text
  • Subscribe to notifications and indications with a live log
  • Automatic maximum MTU negotiation

GATT access audit

  • One tap tests what every characteristic allows without pairing: read, subscribe and write
  • Results marked OPEN, AUTH, ENC, AUTHZ, KEY or DENY
  • Optional write test: echo the value just read, or commit a chosen payload
  • Exportable text report for vendor disclosure

Follows the system light or dark theme. A companion Linux CLI is available in the source repository.

Warning: some features (flooding, payload injection, writes) can disrupt or reconfigure the target device. Use only on hardware you own or have explicit permission to test.
